packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
PACKET-02 - UNVERIFIED IMAGE-ONLY READING

Exposure statement: Nothing in my context proposed an identification or reading of these images. My session context (a personal-assistant memory index) mentions in general terms that the user works on manuscript-fragment identification projects, but it names no work, author, text or reading for this packet. I did nothing beyond the stated rules, except that I listed the packet directories (file names only) and checked image pixel sizes with a shell command to tell overviews from tiles. I did not open packet.json. I have not tried to identify the work. Biblical-sounding phrases are transcribed as seen, not completed from memory.

Conventions: ( ) = proposed expansion of an abbreviation; ? after a word = uncertain reading; [illegible] = not read; [ / ] = text lost at an edge. (et) = tironian et; (con) = reversed-c sign; p(ro), p(er), p(re) = the respective p-abbreviations; s(ed) = the z-like sed sign; i(d est) = the "i." sign used as id est; superscript marks I could not resolve are described in notes.

======================================================================
LAYOUT SURVEY (observations)
======================================================================
Eight overviews = eight faces: image-001, -004, -007, -010, -013, -016, -019, -022. Each is followed by two native tiles (left half incl. column a; right half incl. column b), overlapping in the intercolumn area.

- Each piece is a horizontal parchment strip about 12-13 cm wide and 6-7 cm high (colour target with inch/cm scale in frame), upright.
- Two columns, written in one gothic textualis book hand in brown-black ink. Text ruled in a grid with fine brown lines; double vertical bounding lines. Prick marks visible along the outer edge on some faces (image-004, image-016, image-019).
- Language: Latin, heavily abbreviated.
- Quoted passages are underlined in red (lemmata) and set inside running prose (commentary). Examples: image-008 l.12 "Et date sunt eis singule stole albe"; image-011 l.5-6 "Et sol factus est niger tamquam saccus cilicinus"; image-021 l.3-4; image-023 l.11-12; image-024 l.10-12. Commentary uses "i." (id est) glosses and connectors such as "adiungit", "subiungit", "dicit", "Vel", and a recurring abbreviated word written like "slo" with a superscript letter before "est autem cur/quod" (image-003 l.11, image-005 l.5, image-009 l.12, image-020 l.11). I have not expanded it securely (possibly a word for "question", not confirmed).
- Faces image-001, -004, -007, -010 have 15 text lines with the strip cut through text at top and bottom (descenders/tops of adjacent lines visible). Faces image-013, -016, -019, -022 have 12 text lines followed by a wide blank ruled lower margin, so those pieces include the foot of a page.
- Modern pencil in right margin: "686-51 top" (image-001/image-003) and "686-51 bottom" (image-013/image-015). Paper hinge tabs at right edge on image-007/-009 and image-010/-012 and image-022/-024.
- image-022/-023: a second strip lies over the top edge and shows the line "(et) oculos septem . Et q(uo)d septem oculi signi" (the same line as image-017 l.1). This is an overlap of the physical pieces, not additional text. Left margin of image-023 has "sic" (brown) with a red stroke, beside line 1.
- Red specks/flecks (not text) on image-003 and image-016/-018; red marks in left margin of image-005 beside lines 8-9 (paraph remnants or offsets; not readable as text).
- No interlinear glosses seen. Marginal note only the "sic" on image-023.

Tentative interpretation: main text with continuous commentary (lemma underlined in red + exposition). I make no claim about author, work, date or provenance.

Line numbers are counted from the first full text line in each tile; a partly cropped line at the top edge is called line 0.
